Mathematical blueprint · arXiv v1

The rectangle CLT in Lean

How accurately can a Gaussian vector approximate the probability that a sum of independent random vectors falls in a rectangle? The paper gives bounds even when the covariance is singular. This blueprint follows the proofs from the probability argument to the corresponding Lean declarations.

Paper by Victor Chernozhukov, Denis Chetverikov, Kengo Kato and Yuta Koike.
Blueprint by GPT-Sol 6.2, prompted by Victor Chernozhukov.

Read Theorem 1Download PDFDownload HTMLPaper on arXiv

To follow the role of Gaussian width, start with Lemma C.2. For the envelope condition, see Lemma E.1. For a formal proof that takes a different route, see Lemma H.1.

Of the 40 named results, Lean checks 39 as stated. In Lemma E.1 it makes explicit that the envelope scale is nonnegative. Conjecture 1 remains open.

Main paper · Sections 1–5

Theorem 1

Unrestricted covariance

When the covariance is singular, the Gaussian still has unit variance in every coordinate direction, and its expected maximum measures how much probability can collect near the boundary of a rectangle.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Under (1), for every admissible s4 in (2),

(3)ρℛ(W,Z)≤Cmin{1,gΣL(δ+s4DL)}.

In particular, the envelope alone gives

(4)ρℛ(W,Z)≤Cmin{1,δgΣLDL}.
Assumptions and notation

Here W=∑iξiW=\sum_i\xi_i is a sum of independent centered vectors with ∥ξi∥∞≤δ\|\xi_i\|_\infty\le\delta. The Gaussian vector ZZ has the same covariance Σ\Sigma, with unit marginal variances. The distance ρℛ\rho_{\mathcal R} is the largest discrepancy in their probabilities over axis-aligned rectangles. The Gaussian width is gΣ=𝔼∥Z∥∞g_\Sigma=\mathbb{E}\|Z\|_\infty. The two logarithmic factors are L=log(ep)L=\log(ep) and DL=1+max{0,log(1/(δL))}D_L=1+\max\{0,\log(1/(\delta\sqrt L))\}.

Setup and relative moment bounds
Proof outline
  1. Factor the covariance and work on its range. Each rectangle becomes an intersection of half-spaces with unit normals. Lemma 2 replaces its indicator by a logistic function of width hh, at a cost of order hκLh\kappa L, where κ\kappa controls boundary probabilities. Paper passage
  2. Run the Slepian interpolation just long enough to add Gaussian noise of seed size ε=Lh2\varepsilon=Lh^2. Starting from that same law, retain each summand with a time-dependent probability and adjust its amplitude while increasing Gaussian variance. The covariance stays fixed. Proposition 1 controls the change in the smoothed probability along both stages. Paper passage
  3. On the second stage the cubic term has time factor t/(t+ε)t/(t+\varepsilon), whose integral is at most 11. The fourth-order remainder has factor 1/(t+ε)1/(t+\varepsilon), whose integral is log(1+1/ε)\log(1+1/\varepsilon). Using s3≤δs_3\le\delta, balance smoothing against the remainder by taking h=𝖠max{δ,s4DL}h=\mathsf{A}\max\{\delta,\sqrt{s_4D_L}\}. If this width is too large for the seeded estimate, the probability bound by 11 suffices. Paper passage
  4. Lemma C.2 bounds the sum’s expected maximum by C(gΣ+δL)C(g_\Sigma+\delta L), so κ≤CgΣ\kappa\le Cg_\Sigma when δL≤gΣ\delta L\le g_\Sigma. In the other case the proposed bound already dominates an absolute constant. Finally, s4=δ2s_4=\delta^2 gives the envelope-only conclusion. Paper passage

Main paper · Sections 1–5

Corollary 1

Normalized observations

Normalizing each observation by the square root of the sample size turns the uniform observation bound into the summand envelope required by Theorem 1.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Let X1,…,Xn∈ℝp be independent and centered. Suppose ∥Xi∥∞≤B almost surely and n−1∑i𝔼Xij2=1 for every j. Define Wn:=n−1/2∑iXi, let Zn∼N(0,Cov(Wn)), and define gn:=𝔼∥Zn∥∞. Then

(5)ρℛ(Wn,Zn)≤Cmin{1,BgnLn1+log+nBL}.
Proof outline
  1. Set ξi=Xi/n\xi_i=X_i/\sqrt n. The new summands are centered and independent, their sum has unit marginal variances, and their coordinate envelope is δ=B/n\delta=B/\sqrt n. Paper passage
  2. Apply the envelope conclusion of Theorem 1 and substitute this value of δ\delta into DLD_L. The Gaussian target is the one matching the normalized sum, so its width is gng_n. Paper passage

Main paper · Sections 1–5

Corollary 2

Sub-exponential transfer

A common cap makes every observation bounded while preserving the signed-coordinate geometry that controls the Gaussian width.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Let X1,…,Xn∈ℝp be independent and centered, with n−1∑i𝔼Xij2=1 and maxi,j∥Xij∥ψ1≤K, where K≥1. For Wn≔n−1/2∑iXi and a centered Gaussian Zn with the same covariance, define gn:=𝔼∥Zn∥∞ and

ℓn≔log(en),bn≔Kℓnn,Dn≔1+log+1bnL.

Then

(6)ρℛ(Wn,Zn)≤Cmin{1,bngnLDn}.
Proof outline
  1. Cap each coordinate at 4Klog(en)4K\log(en), recenter, and decompose the normalized sum into its capped and discarded parts. Exponential tails bound the discarded marginal variances and the probability of a large maximum displacement. Paper passage
  2. The cap is odd and 1-Lipschitz, so it contracts the second moments of all signed coordinate differences. Sudakov–Fernique comparison bounds the capped Gaussian width by gng_n. In the nontrivial regime, standardization costs at most a factor of 22 in width. Paper passage
  3. Use Theorem 1 on the standardized capped sum. Couple its unstandardized Gaussian target to the original target by matching the full block covariance of the capped and discarded parts. Paper passage
  4. Enlarge and shrink each rectangle by the two displacement bounds. Lemma 1 controls the resulting shell for the original Gaussian by its thickness times gng_n, giving a transfer cost of order bngnLb_ng_nL. Paper passage

Main paper · Sections 1–5

Theorem 2

Polynomial moment envelopes

A moment bound on the largest coordinate permits rare, large observations, and a separate fourth-moment bound measures how much of their size can fall on any particular coordinate.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Let X1,…,Xn∈ℝp be independent and centered, with n−1∑i𝔼Xij2=1 for every j, and let W,Z,L be as in (7), with gΣ:=𝔼∥Z∥∞. For every fixed q>2, there is a constant Cq>0, depending only on q, such that the following statements hold for all n,p≥1 and B≥1.

(i) If the envelope condition (8) holds, then

(10a)ρℛ(W,Z)≤Cqmin{1,BgΣL1−1/q{log(en)}1/2−1/qn1/2−1/q}.

(ii) If the coordinate fourth-moment condition (9) also holds, then

(10b)ρℛ(W,Z)≤Cqmin{1,gΣ[B1/2L3/4n1/4+BL1−1/qn1/2−1/q{log(e+B(n/L)2/q−1/2)}1−1/q]}.

When both moment conditions hold, we may take the smaller of (10a) and (10b).

Proof outline
  1. Condition on the locations and values of the large observations, then apply Theorem 1 to the remaining centered, bounded sum at a translated rectangle. Paper passage
  2. Lemma E.1 controls the translation, and independent Gaussian additions correct the conditional covariance before the truncation level is chosen. Paper passage
  3. With coordinate fourth moments available, Lemma E.2 separates the tail variance from the expected maximum of the large-increment sum, for which Lemma E.5 gives the logarithmic improvement. Paper passage

Corollary 3

Polyhedral transfer

To test whether a vector lies in a polyhedron, we need only its components along the normals to the defining half-spaces.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Let W∈ℝp be centered with covariance Σ, and let Z∼N(0,Σ). For normal vectors ν1,…,νm∈ℝp with σα2:=να⊤Σνα>0, define

Pa:=⋂α=1m{x:να⊤x≤aα},Δm(W,Z):=supa∈ℝm|ℙ(W∈Pa)−ℙ(Z∈Pa)|.

Suppose that, for some J≥1,

(11)∥να∥1≤Jσα(α≤m).

Define the Gaussian width of the standardized projections by

gP:=𝔼maxα≤m|να⊤Z|σα.

Under the bounded-summand assumptions of Theorem 1, bounds (3) and (4) hold for Δm(W,Z), with gΣ replaced by gP and the substitutions

p↦m,δ↦Jδ,s4↦J2s4.

Under the setup (7) and the envelope condition (8), the bound (10a) holds for Δm(W,Z) with

p↦m,B↦JB.

If the coordinate fourth-moment condition (9) also holds, then (10b) holds for Δm(W,Z) with

p↦m,B↦J2B.

Under the assumptions of Corollary 2, the bound (6) holds for Δm(Wn,Zn) with

p↦m,K↦JK.

In each case, L becomes log(em), the Gaussian width becomes gP≤Clog(em), and the auxiliary quantities in the cited bound are recomputed using the substituted parameters. The bounds are uniform over normal vectors satisfying (11) for the given J. Zero-variance inequalities may be deleted unless they exclude both vectors almost surely, in which case the probability difference is zero.

Proof outline
  1. Handle zero-variance projections by the sign of their threshold, then standardize each remaining projection to obtain a lower orthant with Gaussian width gPg_P. Paper passage
  2. The standardized rows have ℓ1\ell_1 norm at most JJ, so the envelope grows by at most JJ and both relative fourth-moment bounds by at most J2J^2. Paper passage
  3. The same row bound gives parameters JBJB and JKJK for the polynomial envelope and sub-exponential cases, while weighted Hölder gives the common parameter J2BJ^2B for Theorem 2(ii). Paper passage

Main paper · Sections 1–5

Lemma 1

Rectangle anti-concentration

A rectangle changes membership when the largest face violation crosses a short interval, so we seek a bound that retains the expected maximum of the face projections.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Let X1,…,Xn∈ℝr be independent centered random vectors, and define V≔∑iXi. Suppose that

∥Xi∥U≤ηalmost surely for every i,Var(uα⋅V)=v>0for every α≤m.

Let R∈ℝr be a random vector independent of the summands. Then, for every a∈ℝm and s>0,

(14)ℙ(V+R∈Aas∖Aa−s)≤Cmin{1,s+ηv𝔼∥V∥U,(s+η)L/v}.

If instead V is a centered Gaussian vector with Var(uα⋅V)=v>0 for every α, then, for every R independent of V,

(15)ℙ(V+R∈Aas∖Aa−s)≤min{1,2sv𝔼∥V∥U}≤Cmin{1,sL/v}.

The constant C is absolute.

Proof outline
  1. First normalize the common face variance to 11. Pair every bounded summand with an independent copy and select a member of each pair with an independent sign. Given the pairs, the sum is a fixed shift plus a Rademacher sum. Paper passage
  2. If all conditional face variances are at least 1/41/4, Lemma C.1 bounds the shell probability. Symmetrization and contraction of the squared coefficients bound the exceptional probability by a constant times the envelope times the same expected maximum. Exponential moments give the logarithmic alternative. Paper passage
  3. For the Gaussian assertion, smooth the maximum of the affine face violations. Gaussian integration by parts and convexity control the expectation of the derivative of a ramp by the expected face maximum. The active normal has unit length almost surely after duplicate directions are merged, so the limit recovers the shell probability. Paper passage
  4. Rescale to variance vv. Conditioning on the independent shift only translates the thresholds, and the bounds just proved hold for every threshold vector. Paper passage

Main paper · Sections 1–5

Lemma 2

Smoothing error

The logistic smoother has an exact interpretation as a rectangle with randomly displaced faces, so anti-concentration can bound the error at each endpoint.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Under (1), with κ defined in (16), for h≥δ, the Kolmogorov distance over rectangles satisfies

(17)ρ≤Mh+ChκL.
Proof outline
  1. Generate the threshold shifts with independent mean-one exponential variables and let RhR_h be the largest absolute shift. The original and perturbed indicators can differ only in the shell obtained by moving every threshold out and in by RhR_h. Paper passage
  2. Conditional on the shifts, Lemma 1 bounds the shell probability for both the sum and its Gaussian target. Each log-ratio of exponentials has tails bounded by 2e−s2e^{-s}, so a union bound over 2p2p faces and tail integration give 𝔼Rh≤ChL\mathbb{E} R_h\le ChL. Paper passage
  3. Average over the shifts, apply the triangle inequality at both endpoints and take the supremum over thresholds. Since h≥δh\ge\delta, the two endpoint errors together cost at most ChκLCh\kappa L. Paper passage

Proposition 1

Initialization and seeded derivative estimates

The comparison starts with very little Gaussian noise, so the proof estimates the derivatives directly near the starting point and uses Gaussian integration by parts once the seed is available.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Under (1) and (2), with κ defined in (16), there are absolute constants 𝖠,C such that, for h≥𝖠δ, uniformly over a∈ℝm and 0<v<1,

(21)|𝔼D3Fa,h(Tv):K3|≤Cs3κh2,|Ra,h0(v)|≤Cs4κh3.

If Lh2<1/4, choose ε=Lh2 in (18). Then

(22)Ih≤Cs3κL+Cs4κLh,

and, uniformly over a∈ℝm and 0<t<1,

(23)|t3(1+ε)3/2𝔼D3Fa,h(Ut):K3|≤Cs3κLtt+ε,|R4,a,h(t)|≤Cs4κLh(t+ε).
Proof outline
  1. Apply Lemma B.1 on the Slepian path. Sum the signed third moments at a common point and move the positive logistic weights in the fourth-order terms back to that point. The relative moment bounds supply s3s_3 and s4s_4. Paper passage
  2. At every Slepian time, one independent component carries at least half the face variance. Lemmas 1 and A.1 therefore bound the mean logistic weight F(1−F)F(1-F) by ChκCh\kappa. Integrating the resulting direct estimates over the initial interval of length at most Lh2Lh^2 gives the initialization bound. Paper passage
  3. On the calibrated path, split the Gaussian into two independent equal-variance parts. Keep one in the base to establish its boundary bound by Lemma 1, and use the other in Lemma B.2. The signed cubic matrix and the same-copy and independent-copy fourth-moment matrices give the respective moment factors. Paper passage
  4. The paired Gaussian derivatives contribute (t+ε)−1(t+\varepsilon)^{-1}. The calibrated third moment has multiplier 1−t21-t^2, whose derivative supplies the extra factor tt in the cubic bound. The fourth-order remainder retains the full reciprocal. Paper passage

Theorem 4

Centrally symmetric lower bound

Central symmetry cancels every third moment, yet a maximum over many rare coordinates can still give a rectangle error of order BngΣnLn/nB_n g_{\Sigma_n}L_n/\sqrt n.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Let rn,mn,pn,wn be as in (30), let Bn≥2, and suppose that

BnwnLnn→0.

For all sufficiently large n, there are i.i.d. centered, centrally symmetric observations with unit marginal variances, ∥Xn,i∥∞≤Bn, and width satisfying (31), such that

(33)ρℛ(Wn,Zn)≥cBngΣnLnn,

where c>0 is an absolute constant.

Proof outline
  1. In Lemma F.3, activate the rare signs together with probability log(mn)/(2n)\log(m_n)/(2n) and choose amplitude a=Bn−1a=B_n-1 to respect the envelope. Paper passage
  2. With high probability one coordinate receives a positive sign at every activation, giving a mean rare shift asymptotic to alog(mn)/(2n)a\log(m_n)/(2\sqrt n), half its Gaussian counterpart. Paper passage
  3. Lemma F.2 multiplies this mean gap by a leading density of order wnw_n, while the Rademacher approximation from Lemma F.1 and the quadratic shift error are smaller. Paper passage

Conjecture 1

Sharp rectangle approximation under unrestricted covariance

The bounded-summand upper and lower bounds leave open whether the extra square-root logarithm can be removed for every covariance matrix.

Open conjecture Manuscript statement

Under (1), there is an absolute constant C such that

ρℛ(W,Z)≤Cmin{1,δgΣL},L=log(ep),

where gΣ=𝔼∥Z∥∞. The bound holds uniformly in n,p,δ and Σ, including singular Σ.

Why the question is open
  1. Theorem 4 attains the proposed scale δgΣL\delta g_\Sigma L on symmetric examples whose Gaussian widths range from constant order to order L\sqrt L. Paper passage
  2. Theorem 1 gives this rate when s4DLs_4D_L is at most a constant times δ2\delta^2, while the unrestricted assertion remains open and is excluded from the Lean certificate. Paper passage

Corollary 4

Approximation under a positive correlation gap

A positive gap between the absolute correlations of distinct coordinates and 1 gives a second estimate of the interpolation error, even when the covariance matrix is singular.

Under (1), define

Corollary 5

An exceptional correlation budget

The exceptional correlation budget measures how much we pay for pairs below a chosen gap, taking advantage of the exact cancellation at perfect correlation.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Under (1), fix a cutoff c∈(0,1] and define

ηjk:=1−|Σjk|,Bc:=∑1≤j<k≤p0<ηjk<cηjk,Jc:=1+log(1/c).

The empty sum is zero. There is an absolute constant C, independent of the cutoff, such that

Proof outline
  1. Separate the single-face and well-separated pair terms from the pairs with 0<ηjk<c0<\eta_{jk}<c. Lemma G.2 bounds each exceptional signed pair by Cδ2ηjk/h2C\delta^2\sqrt{\eta_{jk}}/h^2, and each original coordinate pair accounts for at most four choices of signs. A zero-gap pair contributes zero. Paper passage
  2. Keep all faces in the logistic weights. In the sum of nonnegative matrix norms in Proposition H.2, retain only the separated pairs and use ϑjksinϑjk≥c(2−c)\vartheta_{jk}\sin\vartheta_{jk}\ge c(2-c) there. Combine this estimate with Proposition H.1 and the translated-weight expansion from the proof of Lemma H.3. Paper passage
  3. Compare the early bound for the whole remainder with this separated-pair estimate and add the exceptional cost. Time integration gives terms of order δ2κLJc/h\delta^2\kappa L J_c/h and δ2Bc/h2\delta^2 B_c/h^2. Paper passage
  4. Balance each term against the smoothing cost κLh\kappa Lh and take the larger of the two resulting widths. Lemma C.2 converts the boundary coefficient to the Gaussian width in the resulting bound. Paper passage

Lemma A.1

Averaging the derivative envelope

Although a logistic derivative may be large near a face, averaging recovers one power of the smoothing width because only a thin shell contributes.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Suppose that U∈ℝr satisfies, for all a∈ℝm and s>0,

ℙ{U∈Aas∖Aa−s}≤C0κ(s+δ),

where κ≥1 and C0 is an absolute constant. Uniformly over thresholds, for h≥4δ,

(A.3)𝔼F(U)(1−F(U))≤Chκ.

Consequently, for each fixed positive integer q, fixed directions z1,…,zq∈ℝr, and h≥max{4δ,𝜚},

(A.4)𝔼sup∥v∥U≤𝜚|DqF(U+v)[z1,…,zq]|≤Cqh1−qκ∏j=1q∥zj∥U.

The constants depend only on C0 and, for Cq, on q.

Proof outline
  1. Shift every threshold by the same amount ss, and denote the new smoother by FsF_s. Its derivative is Fs(1−Fs)/hF_s(1-F_s)/h. On [−h,h][-h,h] this product stays within a fixed factor of its value at zero, so F(1−F)≤(e/2)(Fh−F−h)F(1-F)\le(e/2)(F_h-F_{-h}). Paper passage
  2. Use the same exponential variables to represent both smoothers. Their difference is the probability of a shell whose paired thresholds always differ by 2h2h. Conditioning on the variables and using the assumed shell estimate gives 𝔼[F(1−F)]≤Chκ\mathbb{E}[F(1-F)]\le Ch\kappa. Paper passage
  3. Insert this estimate in the pointwise bound for translated directional derivatives. With the translations measured in the face norm and bounded by hh, the averaged derivative of order qq costs h1−qκh^{1-q}\kappa times the product of the directional face norms. Paper passage

Lemma B.1

Interpolation identity with a Gaussian seed

Evaluating the third derivatives at one common random point makes cancellation across the summands visible before the error is bounded.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Use the independent centered summands of (B.1), and take G∼N(0,Ir) independent of them. Let ε≥0, let γ:(0,1)→(0,∞) be continuously differentiable, and suppose ϖ(t)≔(1−t)/γ(t)2∈[0,1]. For each t, take independent Bernoulli masks with success probability ϖ(t), independent of the summands and G, and define

(B.7)Yt≔γ(t)∑i𝔹i,tζi0+t+εG,Hi,t≔Yt−γ(t)𝔹i,tζi0.

Thus Cov(Yt)={ϖ(t)γ(t)2+t+ε}Ir=(1+ε)Ir, and Hi,t is independent of the removed summand and its mask. No coupling of the masks across different times is required.

To express the Taylor remainders along segments that insert a summand, let ζi,ζ̃i be copies of ζi0, with all copies mutually independent and independent of the original summands, masks, and Gaussian vector. Recall the aggregate third-moment tensor K3, and define the two scalar functions used in the coefficients by

K3=∑i𝔼(ζi0)⊗3,q3(t)≔(1−t)γ(t),ηt≔(1−t)γ′(t)γ(t).

In particular, q3(t)=ϖ(t)γ(t)3 is the multiplier of each retained summand's third-moment tensor.

For a smooth function f:ℝr→ℝ with bounded derivatives through order four, the following identity holds for 0<t<1:

(B.8)ddt𝔼f(Yt)=q3′(t)6𝔼D3f(Yt):K3+∫01∑i𝔼[D4f(Hi,t+sγ(t)ζi):𝒯i,t(s)]ds,

where

𝒯i,t(s)≔at(s)ζi⊗4+bt(s)ζ̃i⊗2⊗ζi⊗2+ct(s)ζ̃i⊗3⊗ζi

and

(B.9)at(s)≔γ(t)26(1−s)2{ηt−1+(1+2ηt)s},bt(s)≔1−t2(1−s),ct(s)≔1−t6(1−ηt).

The colon contracts all corresponding indices. The symmetry of D4f makes explicit symmetrization of the tensors unnecessary.

Proof outline
  1. Differentiate the expectation over the Gaussian variance, the Bernoulli retention probabilities and the retained amplitudes. The Gaussian heat identity gives a Hessian. For each mask, remove that summand and average the change conditional on the remaining base. Paper passage
  2. Taylor-expand along the segment that reinserts an independent copy. Centering removes the linear terms, and the relation ϖ(t)γ(t)2=1−t\varpi(t)\gamma(t)^2=1-t cancels the second-order contribution against the Gaussian Hessian. Paper passage
  3. Restore the removed summand in the Hessian and move the cubic derivative to the full point. Its signed coefficient is q3′(t)/6q_3'(t)/6 with q3(t)=(1−t)γ(t)q_3(t)=(1-t)\gamma(t). The fourth derivatives on the insertion segments give the three displayed kernels, with one or two independent copies as specified. Paper passage

Lemma B.2

Paired derivatives at translated bases

The fourth-order remainder evaluates derivatives at different translated points, but the moment assumptions control sums of matrices at a common Gaussian base.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Let ℋ be a σ-field, let V0 be an ℋ-measurable concentrated base with coefficient κ, and let G∼N(0,Ir) be independent of ℋ. Suppose that δL≤σ≤1, and define U≔V0+σG. Fix s∈{1,2} and b≥0. Let (Zi,Zi,1,…,Zi,s,vi)i be random arrays which, conditional on ℋ, are independent of G. They may depend on ℋ and on one another. Suppose that, almost surely,

(B.18)∑i𝔼[ZiZi⊤∣ℋ]≼Ir,∥Zi,a∥U≤δ(a≤s),∥vi∥U≤bδ.

There are constants 𝖠b,Cb, depending only on b, such that, for F=Fa,h and h≥𝖠bδ,

(B.19)|∑i𝔼Ds+2F(U+vi)[Zi,Zi,Zi,1,…,Zi,s]|≤Cbσ2δsh1−sκL.

The constants are uniform over the threshold vector a.

The factor δs can be replaced by a constant Ms≥0 under the following additional moment bounds. For s=1, suppose that vi=0 for every i and, almost surely, for every face normal uj,

(B.20)∥∑i𝔼[ZiZi⊤(uj⋅Zi,1)∣ℋ]∥op≤M1.

For s=2, suppose that, almost surely, for each a=1,2 and each face normal uj,

(B.21)∑i𝔼[ZiZi⊤(uj⋅Zi,a)2∣ℋ]≼M2Ir.
Proof outline
  1. Condition on the base, translations and directions. Two integrations by parts in the repeated direction replace two derivatives by a centered Gaussian quadratic form divided by σ2\sigma^2. Expand the one or two remaining derivatives into products of face probabilities. Paper passage
  2. Expand each translated logistic weight around the common base, using the small ratio between the translation and hh to obtain a convergent series. Now collect the directional coefficients across observations before estimating the Gaussian averages. Paper passage
  3. The conditional covariance bound controls those coefficient matrices in operator norm. With zero shifts the signed cubic moment gives the sharper first-order factor, and the two weighted fourth-moment bounds give the sharper second-order factor. Paper passage
  4. Pair the coefficient matrices with the Gaussian matrices by operator–nuclear norm duality. Lemma B.4 bounds the sum of the latter norms after averaging the base. Summing the series restores the powers of hh and σ\sigma in the result. Paper passage

Lemma B.3

Gaussian mean relative to a single face

A reference weight depending on a single face lets us control the displacement of a tilted Gaussian mean by the mass lost relative to that face.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Let u∈ℝr be a unit vector and β:ℝ→[0,1] be a measurable function. Denote b(g)≔β(u⋅g) for all g∈ℝr. Also, let w:ℝr→[0,1] be a measurable function satisfying w(g)≤b(g) for all g∈ℝr. In addition, suppose pb≔𝔼b(G)>0 and pw≔𝔼w(G)>0, where G∼N(0,Ir), and let μw≔𝔼[Gw(G)]/pw. Then

(B.25)pw∥μw∥2≤𝔼[w(G)(u⋅G)2]+2pwlog(pb/pw).
Proof outline
  1. Normalize the weight ww to a probability law. For a vector tt perpendicular to the face normal, Jensen’s inequality and w≤bw\le b bound the exponential moment by that of the reference weight. Under the Gaussian law its normal coordinate is independent of t⋅Gt\cdot G. Paper passage
  2. Choose tt to be the orthogonal component of the tilted mean. This bounds its squared length by 2log(pb/pw)2\log(p_b/p_w). Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the remaining normal component by its weighted second moment, and the orthogonal decomposition gives the result. Paper passage

Main paper · Appendices A–F

Lemma B.4

Matrix estimate for logistic weights

Products of logistic face weights couple the Gaussian second derivative to the event of being near the boundary, so their summed matrix norms require an estimate independent of rank.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Let V0∈ℝr satisfy the concentrated-base bound (B.3) with coefficient κ, and let G∼N(0,Ir) be independent of V0. Suppose that δL≤σ≤1 and h≥δ, and define U≔V0+σG. There is an absolute constant C1≥1 such that, for every threshold vector a∈ℝm and every integer k≥1,

(B.28)𝔼V0∑α1,…,αk=1m∥𝔼G[(GG⊤−Ir)Fa,h(U)∏b=1kπαb(U)]∥*≤C1k+1hκL.

Here πj are the face probabilities associated with Fa,h, the sum runs over ordered face tuples, and ∥⋅∥* is the nuclear norm.

Proof outline
  1. Each logistic product defines a log-concave tilt of Gaussian measure. Prékopa’s theorem bounds its covariance by the identity. This reduces the nuclear norm estimate to tilted mean terms and a signed trace summed over face tuples. Paper passage
  2. Compare each tilted mean to a reference depending on its first face. Lemma B.3, Gaussian projection moments and the log-sum inequality bound the total mean contribution using the concentration of the base. Paper passage
  3. Sum the signed trace over the face tuples before taking its absolute value. A common threshold derivative and a Gamma mixture express the result through Gaussian integrals over rectangles with random thresholds. Lemma B.5 controls these derivatives for independent normals. Paper passage
  4. Adjoin a separate, small orthogonal component to each normal so that the enlarged normals are independent. Let the perturbation tend to zero and compress the matrix to its original coordinates. The scale condition σ≥δL\sigma\ge\delta\sqrt L reduces the resulting bound to the stated order. Paper passage

Lemma B.5

Averaged Gaussian threshold derivative

A common movement of all thresholds differentiates a Gaussian integral over a polyhedron, and the faces and their pairwise intersections determine the derivative.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Suppose the unit normal vectors u1,…,um are linearly independent and let V0 be a concentrated base with coefficient κ. Take G∼N(0,Ir) independent of V0. Fix σ>0 and let J(b) and 𝒟(b) be defined as in (B.38). Also, for every a∈ℝm, define bj(V0):=(aj−uj⋅V0)/σ, j=1,…,m. Then

(B.41)𝔼[|𝒟(b(V0))|]≤Cκ(σL+δL3/2).
Proof outline
  1. Differentiate the Gaussian variance and, independently, rescale the thresholds. Equating the two expressions for the derivative gives the radial trace identity. Differentiate it in all thresholds together and condition on one Gaussian projection to express the result using first and mixed second derivatives of the Gaussian distribution function. Paper passage
  2. Interpret these nonnegative derivatives as Gaussian masses on faces and intersections of two faces. Extend each stratum a short distance outwards along its normal directions. A point in any such region has a unique nearest point on the polyhedron, so the regions are disjoint. Paper passage
  3. Let R(G)R(G) be one plus the largest norm of a projection onto a subspace spanned by one or two face normals. The regions lie in an outer shell of width 1/R(G)1/R(G) in Gaussian coordinates. Conditional on GG, concentration of the independent base bounds this shell by Cκ(σ/R(G)+δ)C\kappa(\sigma/R(G)+\delta). Paper passage
  4. The geometric estimate weights that shell by R(G)3R(G)^3. Gaussian projection moments bound the expected square and cube by CLCL and CL3/2CL^{3/2}, respectively, giving the claimed derivative estimate. Paper passage

Lemma C.1

Rademacher boundary estimate

On the discrete cube, changes along edges reveal how often the maximum of affine functions can fall in a short interval, even when an endpoint carries an atom.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Let ε be uniform on {−1,1}n, and let b1,…,bm∈ℝn satisfy minα∥bα∥22≥σ2>0 and maxα,i|bαi|≤b. For thresholds a1,…,am, define

F(x):=maxα≤m(bα⋅x−aα),ℳ:=𝔼max{0,maxα≤mbα⋅ε}.

Then, for every t∈ℝ and h≥0,

(C.1)ℙ{t≤F(ε)≤t+h}≤h+8bσ2ℳ.

If also maxα∥bα∥22≤1, then ℳ≤2log(m+1).

Proof outline
  1. First perturb the thresholds so the maximizing affine function is unique at each vertex. Compose the maximum with the integral of a ramp whose linear portion extends beyond the interval by an amount set by the largest coefficient. Paper passage
  2. Convexity along a cube edge makes the average signed derivative nonnegative. On edges meeting the interval, this average also bounds the squared active slope divided by the enlarged width. Sum over the coordinates and use the lower bound on the squared length of every active coefficient vector. Paper passage
  3. The same sum of signed derivatives is bounded above by the expected positive maximum of the original linear forms. Compare the two bounds and send the perturbation to zero through enlarged closed intervals. Under the unit-length upper bound, the Rademacher exponential moment and Jensen’s inequality give the logarithmic estimate. Paper passage

Lemma E.1

An expected maximum under an envelope moment

To estimate the shift left by conditioning on large observations, we need a bound on the expected maximum that uses both a coordinate variance budget and a moment bound on the envelope.

Checked for A ≥ 0 Manuscript statement

Let Y1,…,Yn be independent centered vectors in ℝp. If

maxj∑i𝔼Yij2≤v,∑i𝔼∥Yi∥∞q≤Aq,q>2,

then

(E.2)𝔼∥∑iYi∥∞≤Cq{vL+AL1−1/q}.

Envelope condition. Lean assumes A ≥ 0. The proof handles zero separately and uses a positive truncation level in the other case. The application takes the nonnegative root of the moment bound.

Proof outline
  1. The envelope scale AA must be nonnegative, as the checked statement makes explicit. If A=0A=0, the moment bound forces every vector to vanish almost surely. Paper passage
  2. For A>0A>0, truncate at u=AL−1/qu=AL^{-1/q} and center each retained vector. The coordinate variance sums are at most vv, and the summand envelope is at most 2u2u. Paper passage
  3. Apply Bernstein’s inequality to the 2p2p signed coordinates and integrate the tail to get a bound of order vL+uL\sqrt{vL}+uL. The omitted centered sum costs at most 2Aqu1−q2A^q u^{1-q}, and the cutoff makes both envelope contributions of order AL1−1/qAL^{1-1/q}. Paper passage

Lemma E.2

Gaussian comparison with large-increment remainders

The Bennett refinement needs to keep the expected maximum of the sum of large copy differences intact until both moment assumptions can be brought to bear.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

There is an absolute constant C>0 with the following property. Let n,p≥1, and let X1,…,Xn∈ℝp be independent centered random vectors with finite coordinate fourth moments and n−1∑i𝔼Xij2=1 for every j≤p. Define

W:=n−1/2∑iXi,Σ:=Cov(W),Z∼N(0,Σ),L:=log(ep).

Let X̃i be mutually independent copies of Xi, independent of the original array, and define

Yi:=(X̃i−Xi)/n,Δ1:=1n2maxj∑i𝔼Xij4.

For t>0, define

vt:=maxj∑i𝔼[Yij2𝟏{∥Yi∥∞>t}],Mt:=𝔼∥∑iYi𝟏{∥Yi∥∞>t}∥∞.

With gΣ:=𝔼∥Z∥∞, for every ϕ>0,

(E.10)ρℛ(W,Z)≤CgΣL{Lϕ+ϕL2Δ1+ϕ3L7/2Δ1+ϕL3/2vt+LMt},t:=(ϕL)−1.

The covariance may be singular, and the observations need not be identically distributed or symmetric.

Proof outline
  1. Apply Lemma E.4 to the logistic rectangle approximation at cutoff h=(ϕL)−1h=(\phi L)^{-1}, bounding the large-increment drift by MhM_h in expected norm and the covariance bias by vh/2v_h/2 entrywise. Paper passage
  2. To use coordinate fourth moments in the remainder, move the positive logistic weights to a common evaluation point before summing over observations. Paper passage
  3. Average the derivative bounds with the Gaussian boundary estimate from Lemmas A.1 and 1, then integrate in time and recover rectangle probabilities by Lemma E.3. Paper passage

Lemma E.3

Smoothing from the Gaussian endpoint

Smoothing must recover rectangle probabilities even when only the Gaussian endpoint has a known boundary-concentration estimate.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Let V∈ℝp be any random vector, and let Z∈ℝp be centered Gaussian with Var(Zj)=1 for every j≤p. Define gΣ:=𝔼∥Z∥∞. Then, for every h>0,

(E.11)ρℛ(V,Z)≤C{supa∈ℝ2p|𝔼Fa,h(V)−𝔼Fa,h(Z)|+hgΣL},L:=log(ep),

where C is absolute.

Proof outline
  1. The logistic mixture expresses the smooth discrepancy as an average over random threshold shifts, all of magnitude at most d=KhLd=KhL with probability at least 3/43/4 for a suitable absolute KK. Paper passage
  2. Expand or contract the rectangle according to the discrepancy’s sign, using monotonicity for the arbitrary vector and Lemma 1 to bound the Gaussian boundary layer. Paper passage
  3. Absorb the exceptional shifts using their probability bound, which the paper obtains by Markov’s inequality and Lean derives directly from the exponential variables. Paper passage

Lemma E.4

Slepian interpolation with paired increments

Pairing each summand with an independent copy turns its contribution to the interpolation derivative into a difference of gradients, even for skewed summands.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Under the assumptions and notation of Lemma E.2, take Z independent of the original array and its copies. For h>0, define 𝒳:=σ(X1,…,Xn) and

Y‾i:=Yi𝟏{∥Yi∥∞≤h},bh:=𝔼[∑iYi𝟏{∥Yi∥∞>h}∣𝒳],Th:=12∑i𝔼[Y‾iY‾i⊤∣𝒳].

Along the Slepian path Ws:=sW+1−sZ, 0≤s≤1, every C4 function f:ℝp→ℝ with bounded derivatives of orders 1 through 4 satisfies, for 0<s<1,

(E.12)dds𝔼f(Ws)=12𝔼[(Th−Σ):D2f(Ws)]−12s𝔼[bh⋅∇f(Ws)]−s8∑i𝔼∫01r(1−r)D4f(Ws+rsY‾i)[Y‾i,Y‾i,Y‾i,Y‾i]dr.

Here A:B:=∑j,kAjkBjk for matrices A,B.

Proof outline
  1. Differentiate along Ws=sW+1−sZW_s=\sqrt{s}\,W+\sqrt{1-s}\,Z and integrate by parts in the Gaussian coordinates to obtain the covariance–Hessian term. Paper passage
  2. Swapping a summand with its copy reverses the increment, pairing gradients at the segment endpoints for retained increments and leaving a conditional drift from discarded increments. Paper passage
  3. Apply the trapezoidal identity to the directional Hessian along that segment, using equality of endpoint expectations to leave a fourth-derivative remainder with coefficient −s/8-s/8. Paper passage

Suppose independent centrally symmetric vectors Ti∈ℝp satisfy maxj∑i𝔼Tij2≤v and ∑i𝔼∥Ti∥∞q≤Aq, with q>1. For every u>0 and v>0,

Lemma F.1

Uniform scalar moderate-tail estimate

To detect skewness at the threshold of a high-dimensional maximum, we need a relative error for the strict scalar tail that also applies to lattice laws.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Let S:=∑i=1nηi, where the real variables ηi are independent and centered, δ>0, |ηi|≤δ almost surely, and ∑i𝔼ηi2=1. Write γ:=∑i𝔼ηi3. There are absolute constants c0,C>0 such that, whenever x≥0 and δ(1+x)≤c0,

(F.1)|logℙ(S>x)1−Φ(x)−γx36|≤C{δ(1+x)+δ2x4}.

The tail is strict. The conclusion includes lattice distributions and has constants independent of the lattice spacing or the position of x relative to its atoms.

Proof outline
  1. Tilt the product law so the sum has mean xx, and use bounds on the tilted variance and fourth cumulant to expand its log moment-generating function. Paper passage
  2. Apply Berry–Esseen to the standardized tilted sum and integrate its strict upper tail against an exponential weight, preserving the endpoint convention at atoms. Paper passage
  3. Undoing the tilt and comparing with the weighted normal integral leaves γx3/6\gamma x^3/6 as the leading log tail correction, where γ\gamma sums the third moments. Paper passage

The symmetric examples create an orthant discrepancy from a difference in the mean shifts of two approximately equal leading maxima.

Let A and G be real random variables such that the distribution function F of G is twice continuously differentiable with ∥F″∥∞<∞, and suppose that, for some ϵ≥0, supx|ℙ(A≤x)−F(x)|≤ϵ. Let U be independent of A, and let V be independent of G, with 𝔼U2+𝔼V2<∞. Then, for every t∈ℝ,

(F.9)|ℙ(A+U≤t)−ℙ(G+V≤t)−F′(t)(𝔼V−𝔼U)|≤ϵ+12∥F″∥∞(𝔼U2+𝔼V2).

Proposition G.1

Dimension-logarithm cap

The logarithm in the envelope bound comes from integrating near the start of the path, where the single-face and two-face estimates offer different ways to cut the integral short.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Under (1), define JL:=min{DL,L}. There is an absolute constant C such that

(G.1)ρℛ(W,Z)≤Cmin{1,δgΣLJL}.

Here gΣ=𝔼∥Z∥∞. More precisely, for h≥𝖠δ and ε=Lh2<1/4, the remainder in (20) satisfies

(G.2)supa∫01|R4,a,h(t)|dt≤Cδ2κLhmin{1+log(1/ε),L}.
Proof outline
  1. With v=t+εv=t+\varepsilon, compare the v−1v^{-1} estimate from Proposition 1 separately with the v−3/2v^{-3/2} single-face bound and the v−1/2v^{-1/2} pair bound in Lemma G.2. Integrate each minimum on the two sides of its crossing point. Paper passage
  2. Because ε=Lh2\varepsilon=Lh^2, the width cancels from both logarithmic ratios. The remaining ratios grow at most polynomially in pp, since there are 2p2p faces and the support rank is at most pp. Direct integration also gives 1+log(1/ε)1+\log(1/\varepsilon), so we can keep the smaller logarithm. Paper passage
  3. Use this estimate for the normalized fourth-order remainder in the smoothing comparison and choose hh proportional to δmin(DL,L)\delta\sqrt{\min(D_L,L)}. Lemma C.2 supplies the Gaussian width, and the elementary probability bound covers the large-width case. The cap applies to the envelope estimate with s4=δ2s_4=\delta^2. Paper passage

Lemma G.1

Concentration for one or two face projections

Concentration in two face projections depends on their angle because nearly parallel normals impose nearly the same restriction.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Let V=∑iXi+GA, where the Xi∈ℝr are independent and centered, ∥Xi∥U≤bδ, and GA is an independent centered Gaussian vector. Suppose Cov(V)=τ2Ir, with c0≤τ2≤C0. There are constants A,C, depending only on b,c0,C0, such that, for h≥Aδ,

(G.3)supxℙ{|uj⋅V−x|≤h}≤Ch,
(G.4)supx,yℙ{|uj⋅V−x|≤h,|uk⋅V−y|≤h}≤Ch2/νjk,νjk:=1−(uj⋅uk)2>0.

For the logistic weights Wj=Fπj and Wjk=Fπjπk at width h and arbitrary thresholds, these estimates imply

(G.5)supz𝔼Wj(V+z)≤Ch,supz𝔼Wjk(V+z)≤Ch2/νjk,

with the second bound for νjk>0. The bounds also hold after an independent random shift.

Proof outline
  1. Use the first normal and the normalized orthogonal component of the second as coordinates. A box of width hh in each original face coordinate has widths of order hh and h/νjkh/\nu_{jk} in these coordinates. Paper passage
  2. On the corresponding frequency rectangle, the projected summands have small phases. Symmetrizing with independent copies bounds the characteristic function by a Gaussian exponential. A product of squared sinc kernels then bounds the box probability by Ch2/νjkCh^2/\nu_{jk}. A single kernel gives the one-face bound. Paper passage
  3. Bound each logistic weight by an integrable function of its one or two scores and sum the concentration bounds on unit score cells. The estimates are uniform in the thresholds, so conditioning permits any independent random shift. Paper passage
  4. Lean carries out the Fourier estimate in the original correlated coordinates, completing a square to recover the same angle factor. It bounds the logistic weights with exponential majorants and averages over overlapping unit boxes. Paper passage

Lemma G.2

As two normals approach parallelism, the two-face concentration bound worsens, but the coefficient multiplying that pair in the Hessian approaches zero.

Let h≥Aδ, ε=Lh2<1/4, and v:=t+ε. Along the calibrated interpolation,

(G.8)|R4,single,a,h(t)|≤Cmrδ2v−3/2,
(G.9)|R4,jk,a,h(t)|≤Cmin{δ2νjkh2,rδ2νjkv},νjk>0.

Parallel or antiparallel pairs contribute zero. Consequently,

(G.10)|R4,a,h(t)|≤Cmrδ2v3/2+Cm2rδ2hv.

  1. Expand the Hessian into single-face terms and pair terms. For a nonparallel pair, resolving the coefficient along the normalized difference of the signed normals extracts 1−|uj⋅uk|1-|u_j\cdot u_k|. Lemma G.1 then gives a pair bound proportional to δ2νjk/h2\delta^2\nu_{jk}/h^2. Paper passage
  2. For a second estimate, transfer the repeated derivatives to the independent Gaussian component. Expand each translated weight at a common base before taking absolute values, so that the covariance sum still controls the signed coefficient matrix. Paper passage
  3. The Gaussian matrix moments and Lemma G.1 give bounds proportional to mrδ2v−3/2mr\delta^2 v^{-3/2} for the single-face sum and rδ2/(νjkv)r\delta^2/(\nu_{jk}v) for a nonparallel pair. The geometric mean of the two pair bounds removes νjk\nu_{jk}. Sum over pairs, observing that the coefficient vanishes for parallel or antiparallel normals. Paper passage

Lemma H.1

Two localized surface estimates

The geometric estimate controls two signed Gaussian surface integrals, one over actual facets and one over ridges, without a lower bound on the angles between normals.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Let V satisfy (H.6), and let Q=P(a) be empty or full dimensional. For every 0<σ≤1, define (Q−V)/σ:={g:V+σg∈Q}. Then

(H.10)𝔼|Jf((Q−V)/σ)|+𝔼|Je((Q−V)/σ)|≤Cκ(σL3/2+δL2).

The constant depends only on C0, and no angle separation is needed.

Two proof routes. Lean obtains the all-threshold surface bound by continuity and Fatou’s lemma. The nonsimple-ridge Gauss–Green identity and the spherical conormal identity for any number of edges have separate Lean proofs. For the spherical identity Lean uses Gaussian first moments and polar coordinates. The printed tangent-field and divergence calculation at lines 1112–1123 remains outside that correspondence. H.1 completion record

Proof outline
  1. For every threshold list whose polyhedron is empty or has nonempty interior in the ambient support space, the lemma bounds the sum of the two expected absolute values. It allows 0<σ≤10<\sigma\le1, any number of facets at a codimension-three face, and bases satisfying the stated boundary concentration inequality. Paper passage
  2. In the printed proof, Gauss–Green on neighboring facets pairs their ridge contributions. Gauss–Green on the ridges gives (H.14), and spherical divergence gives (H.15), which bounds the sum of the angle-weighted conormals by twice the spherical polygon’s area. Short disjoint outward tubes turn these integrals into a boundary probability. Gaussian projection moments and concentration of the base then give the stated bound. Paper passage
  3. Lean proves the all-threshold bound by fixing the actual facets of the target and proving the ridge estimate at almost every nearby threshold. The ridge integral is continuous at the target for each fixed base value. Fatou’s lemma passes the expected absolute value to the limit, even for a singular base law. Paper passage
  4. The addendum separately proves the pointwise nonsimple ridge identity (H.14) and the conormal identity (H.15) for a complete spherical polygon with arbitrarily many edges. Its proof of (H.15) uses a Gaussian first moment and polar coordinates. The printed tangent-field calculation is a distinct derivation. The formal surface measures use Euclidean orthonormal charts and polar angular measure. Paper passage

Supplement · Appendices G–I

Lemma H.2

Gaussian matrices and projected reference weights

To estimate the Gaussian matrix left by integration by parts, we reduce its nuclear norm to a signed trace and the mean under a weighted Gaussian law.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Let G∼N(0,Ir), and let w≥0 have positive Gaussian mass pw:=𝔼w(G) and finite Gaussian second moments. Define the weighted probability law and its mean and covariance by

dPw(g):=w(g)φr(g)pwdg,μw:=𝔼Pwg,Kw:=CovPw(g).

If w is log-concave and w(g)≤Cw(1+∥g∥), then Kw≼Ir and

(H.21)∥𝔼[(GG⊤−Ir)w(G)]∥*≤2pw∥μw∥2−𝔼[(∥G∥2−r)w(G)].

If instead, or in addition, w≤b, where b depends only on an orthogonal projection Πg and pb:=𝔼b(G)<∞, then

(H.22)pw∥μw∥2≤𝔼[w(G)∥ΠG∥2]+2pwlog(pb/pw).

Zero-mass weights may be omitted from either inequality.

Proof outline
  1. For a log-concave weight, the Gaussian convolution is log-concave by Prékopa’s theorem. At zero the Hessian of its logarithm equals the tilted covariance minus the identity, so the tilted covariance is bounded above by the identity. Paper passage
  2. Write the matrix as the difference of the positive mean outer product and the positive covariance deficit, each multiplied by the mass of the weight. The traces of those positive matrices bound the nuclear norm while keeping the original signed trace. Paper passage
  3. For the separate mean estimate, dominate the weight by a reference depending only on the projected Gaussian. Jensen’s inequality and independence of the orthogonal component give the logarithm of the ratio of the two masses. Cauchy–Schwarz controls the mean within the projected subspace. Paper passage

Supplement · Appendices G–I

Proposition H.1

Single-face cubic matrix estimate

The single-face term requires a cubic Gaussian matrix estimate that survives the extra logistic factors produced by translating a weight.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Suppose V satisfies (H.6), G∼N(0,Ir) is independent of V, and U=V+σG, with h≥δ and δL≤σ≤1. For every integer k≥1,

(H.24)𝔼V∑α∈[m]k∥𝔼G[ℋ3,uα1(G)Wα(U)]∥*≤Ck+1hκL3/2.

No correlation gap is needed for this estimate.

Proof outline
  1. At a fixed base value, split the first normal coordinate of the Gaussian into its positive and negative parts. Multiplying each part by the tuple weight gives two log-concave weights to which Lemma H.2 applies. Paper passage
  2. Use a reference weight depending only on that normal coordinate to bound each tilted mean. After summing over tuples and signs, the reference and actual masses share the factor hκh\kappa, which cancels inside the logarithm. Paper passage
  3. Sum the signed traces before taking absolute values. Differentiating powers of the logistic function in the first threshold and using the Gamma–exponential mixture turns the sum into facet integrals. Lemma H.1 bounds them, and the mean estimate controls the two remaining rank-one terms of the cubic matrix. Paper passage

Supplement · Appendices G–I

Proposition H.2

Angle-weighted two-face matrix estimate

The two-face matrix estimate keeps an angle weight until the signed trace has been expressed as an integral over ridges.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Suppose V satisfies (H.6), G∼N(0,Ir) is independent of V, and U=V+σG, with h≥δ and δL≤σ≤1. For every integer K≥2,

(H.27)𝔼V∑α∈[m]K(α1,α2)∈𝒟λα1α2∥𝔼G[(GG⊤−Ir)Wα(U)]∥*≤CK+1h2κL3/2σ.

In particular, under the correlation gap the same sum without the weights λ is at most CK+1h2κL3/2/(dcσ).

Proof outline
  1. Apply Lemma H.2 with a reference weight depending only on the plane spanned by the first two normals. The joint density of the two projections costs 1/sinϑjk1/\sin\vartheta_{jk}, which is canceled by the sine in the angle weight. Paper passage
  2. Differentiate the Gamma–exponential mixture in both thresholds. The positive ridge integrals following Lemma H.1 bound the total weighted mass and its projected second moment. Summing both the actual and reference masses with the same angle weights bounds the tilted means. Paper passage
  3. For the signed trace, the two-threshold coarea formula leaves precisely the exterior angle multiplying each ridge integral. Lemma H.1 bounds the resulting sum. A gap is required only to remove the angle weights, at a cost of 1/[c(2−c)]1/[c(2-c)]. Paper passage

Supplement · Appendices G–I

Lemma H.3

Fourth derivatives at translated concentrated bases

The fourth-order remainder evaluates derivatives at summand-dependent shifts, while the matrix estimates apply at a common Gaussian base.

Checked as stated Manuscript statement

Let ℋ be a sigma-field, let V be an ℋ-measurable concentrated base satisfying (H.6), and let G∼N(0,Ir) be independent of ℋ. Suppose the finite array (Zi,zi,wi,vi)i=1n, with all entries in ℝr, is jointly independent of G conditional on ℋ. For a fixed b≥0, suppose almost surely that

∑i𝔼[ZiZi⊤∣ℋ]≼Ir,∥zi∥U,∥wi∥U≤δ,∥vi∥U≤bδ.

If δL≤σ≤1, there are constants Ab≥1,Cb such that h≥Abδ implies

(H.32)|∑i𝔼D4F(V+σG+vi)[Zi,Zi,zi,wi]|≤Cbdcδ2κL3/2σ3.

The constants depend only on b,C0, and not on the rank. No mutual independence of the entries of an array is required, and vi may depend on the other entries. Concentration (H.6) is required only unconditionally, not after conditioning on ℋ.

Proof outline
  1. Condition on the base information and on the array, so the remaining Gaussian is independent and the directions are fixed. Two integrations by parts remove the repeated derivative. The single-face part of the Hessian requires one more integration and produces the cubic Hermite matrix. Paper passage
  2. Expand the shifted logistic weights in powers of the changes in their exponential scores. At each order the unshifted weights factor out of the conditional average over the array. The aggregate conditional second-moment bound controls the operator norm of the resulting coefficient matrix, even when a shift depends on the directions. Paper passage
  3. Use operator–nuclear norm duality, then apply Proposition H.1 to the single-face terms and Proposition H.2 to the independent pairs. For h≥Abδh\ge A_b\delta the series is summable. The base concentration used by the two propositions is unconditional. Paper passage

Sources and scope

Verification record

This reader accompanies arXiv:2611.21474v1 and its separate supplement. The release tag arxiv-v1-lean-2026-11 identifies commit 8a13fd2. The source manifest records the manuscript hashes, Lean 4.19.0 and the mathematical library revisions.

What was checked

The first clean run built the library and audited the released results. A second run at the same proof commit checked the full types of 1,949 declarations and recorded their dependencies. A later clean run built the whole library with the supplemental H.1 extension, directly checked 66 source modules and audited 182 registered targets. All three records report successful completion. The axiom audits found only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

  • Baseline build and audit
  • Full manuscript mapping and dependency record
  • Clean H.1 extension
  • Reproduction instructions

How to read the evidence

The theorem index identifies the checked conclusion. The proof entries follow the reasoning in the paper and give links to corresponding Lean declarations or documented changes of argument. For example, Lemma E.1 states its sign convention explicitly, and Lemma H.1 distinguishes the proof of a bound from the separately proved identities. Full passage ledger.
